reports.title: Donna Levy: Prevention of future deaths report
categories: Hospital Death (Clinical Procedures and medical management) related deaths

promises.quote: include: increasing nursing capacity; holding weekly multidisciplinary Complex Case discussion meetings; updating the risk escalation process; devising standardised operating procedure relating to how district nurses conduct their daily handovers; providing relevant training for health and social care staff; making the completion of mental capacity assessments in complex cases mandatory; undertaking risk assessments to identify anxiety and depression scores; increasing frequency of high risk cases
promises.summary: increase nursing capacity and improve risk assessments

concerns.quote: Since 2020 Ms Levy had been provided with domiciliary care commissioned by the local authority. At the time of her death twice daily visits were undertaken. Ms Levy was utilising state funded domiciliary care visits to deliver fast food to her home, no personal care was being provided. Carers had escalated to the local authority Ms [name redacted] reluctance to accept personal care and raised safeguarding reports regarding Ms [name redacted] living conditions.
concerns.hazard: lack of personal care and provision of fast food only

concerns.quote: In the two months prior to her final admission into hospital Ms Levy was being regularly assessed by district nurses, the community matron and her GP. Despite the obvious nature of her deteriorating health, no meaningful steps were taken to escalate the care she received to mitigate the risks of her self-neglect.

The inquest heard that as Ms Levy was believed to have capacity throughout this period, and consequently it was determined that there were on practical steps that could have been taken to improve the provision of care to her.
No formal Mental Capacity Act assessment was ever undertaken or considered.
No formal referral was made to mental health services regarding Ms [name redacted] reluctance to take advantage of offered care.

The Trust responsible for community care did not undertake a Serious Investigation. The decision was justified on the basis that Ms [name redacted] pressure sore was insufficiently significant to justify further inquiry. The decision was, in the view of the court flawed as evidence heard indicated that the pressure sore was in fact far more serious than appreciated at the time of community treatment. Further, restricting the scope of a serious incident report to the extent of a single pressure sore, neglected

reports.title: Omar Ahmed: Prevention of Future Deaths Report
categories: Community health care and emergency services related deaths

concerns.quote: Poor standards of communication between the domiciliary care company, the local authority and NHS trust resulted in a failure to identify the deterioration in Mr [name redacted] living conditions and health
concerns.hazard: failure to identify deterioration in living conditions and health

concerns.quote: Evidence heard in the inquest suggested an under-resourced and demoralised district nursing team lacked the clinical curiosity to predict the harm that would befall Mr Ahmed should he be allowed to disengage from treatment
concerns.hazard: lack of clinical curiosity to predict harm

concerns.quote: Mr [name redacted] poor decision-making in how he budgeted was never challenged, this led to a lack of nutritious food and cleaning materials in his home
concerns.hazard: lack of nutritious food and cleaning materials

concerns.quote: Mr [name redacted] unwillingness to turn on his central heating, a contributory factor in the development of his fatal condition -hypothermia, remained unchallenged at the time of his death

Domiciliary carers capitulated to Mr [name redacted] express wishes that they ought not assist him with cleaning, personal care or meals instead, state-funded care hours were utilised to assist Mr Ahmed in attending his local pub and café
concerns.hazard: misuse of care hours for non-care activities

links.explanation: Both reports highlight that domiciliary care funded by the state was being used for non‑care purposes (food delivery or pub/café trips) instead of providing personal care. They also point to inadequate communication and oversight between care providers, commissioners and NHS services as a contributing factor.
